one:
Joane V. Serrano is a thesis adviser with a documented record of supervising six graduate students within the repository, spanning the years 2022 to 2026. Their most recent advisory activity includes an advisee in the latest year, 2026, indicating active engagement with current research topics. Serrano has also contributed thirteen own articles to the repository, demonstrating a consistent scholarly output that intersects with their supervisory interests. The breadth of their research focus is evident in the sub-topics associated with their items, with Gender and inclusion appearing in twelve items, making it the most frequent theme. Other significant areas include Social media, Governance and public policy, and Business and entrepreneurship, each appearing in three items. Additional interests encompass Public health and COVID-19, Culture and identity, Environment and sustainability, Climate and disaster, Management and leadership, and Health communication.

Serrano’s supervision patterns reveal a preference for qualitative and mixed-method approaches to complex social phenomena. In 2026, they advised Czar Ian Angel B. Esquivel on a thesis examining the role of neighborhood talks, or tsismis, in lay discussions of health information in an island barangay in Western Visayas, Philippines. This work utilized thematic analysis and focused on health information, social networks, and social media dynamics. The previous year, 2025, saw two distinct supervisory projects. Aspen Dolene C. Martinez investigated how regional museums in the Visayas contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals through a focused ethnography toward ASEAN Socio-Cultural Collaboration, linking culture, governance, and sustainability. Simultaneously, Carlo Jay F. Ruiz conducted a qualitative case study on campus journalism in Cavite public high schools, exploring stakeholder perspectives on the implementation of journalism programs under the Campus Journalism Act.

In 2024, Serrano supervised a study on mansplaining among women faculty members at a university in Cagayan de Oro City, employing descriptive phenomenology and semi-structured interviews to explore gender dynamics in academia. The 2023 supervision involved Mike C. Antolin, who investigated climate change knowledge, attitudes, and behavioral intentions among employees of a global software company, grounded in the Theory of Reasoned Action. The earliest recorded thesis in this period, from 2022, focused on Filipino domestic workers in Singapore during the COVID-19 pandemic, using hermeneutical phenomenology to understand communication dynamics during social isolation.

Serrano’s own scholarly work reinforces these supervisory themes. Their articles frequently address gender inclusion, particularly within the Philippine Technology Startup Ecosystem, as seen in baseline surveys and case studies on women’s leadership challenges. They have also examined gender voices in ASEAN disaster risk reduction discourse and indigenous peoples’ civil society organizations. Earlier works from 2018 analyzed gender portrayal and fairness in University of the Philippines Open University social media sites and open educational resources. More recent publications from 2026 explore creative responses to sustainability through cultural initiatives. This alignment between their published research and advised theses suggests Serrano is well-equipped to guide students interested in the intersections of gender, communication, policy, and sustainability. Their experience spans diverse contexts, from local barangays in the Philippines to regional ASEAN collaborations and global corporate environments, providing a versatile foundation for thesis supervision.

The breadth of these sub-topics suggests a versatile approach to communication studies, often intersecting with social justice, organizational behavior, and public policy.

In terms of research focus, Serrano demonstrates a consistent attention to how gender dynamics operate within various institutional and social contexts. These works often employ methods such as critical discourse analysis, content analysis, and case studies to uncover disparities in representation and leadership. For instance, research titled "Breaking the Glass Ceiling" investigates challenges and successes for women in leadership positions within the tech sector, while other works explore the gender voice in disaster risk reduction discourse within ASEAN. This focus extends to the intersection of technology and gender, as seen in studies on chatbot gender and user behavior, highlighting a nuanced understanding of how digital tools reflect and reinforce social structures.

Beyond gender, Serrano’s items cover a wide array of contemporary issues. Governance and public policy are explored through studies on ASEAN socio-cultural collaboration and indigenous peoples’ engagement with regional bodies. Environmental and sustainability concerns are addressed in articles discussing creative responses to sustainability and cultural initiatives. The inclusion of public health and COVID-19 topics, along with climate and disaster research, indicates an awareness of global crises and their localized impacts. Social media remains a recurring thread, appearing in studies on gender portrayal and as a sub-topic in advised theses, suggesting a familiarity with digital communication landscapes.

Regarding thesis supervision, Serrano has advised six theses from 2022 to 2026, covering diverse topics that align with their research interests. The advised works include an examination of neighborhood talks in health information dissemination in Western Visayas, which touches on health communication and social networks. Another thesis investigates the role of museums in advancing Sustainable Development Goals through focused ethnography, linking culture and identity with governance and sustainability. Other supervised topics include campus journalism in Cavite public high schools, the phenomenon of mansplaining among women faculty members in Cagayan de Oro City, climate change knowledge among employees in the global software sector, and communication dynamics during social isolation for Filipino domestic workers in Singapore. These supervised projects span qualitative methods such as phenomenology, case studies, and ethnography, reflecting a capacity to guide students through varied methodological approaches. For example, the 2026 thesis on neighborhood talks in Western Visayas utilized thematic analysis to understand informal health communication, while the 2025 study on campus journalism in Cavite employed a qualitative case study approach to examine stakeholder perspectives.
